claims.text: The as-sintered W–Ta–Cr–V–Hf-type refractory HEA has a homogeneous BCC matrix without pre-existing coherent precipitates.
Post-sintering thermal aging can induce stepwise controllable coherent nanoprecipitation in a tungsten-based refractory HEA.
Aging at approximately 900°C for 3–6 hours under inert gas or high vacuum is an appropriate treatment for producing the desired nanoprecipitates.
The aging treatment will produce uniformly distributed, coherent nanoprecipitates within the alloy matrix.
The nanoprecipitate interfaces act as effective sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
Coherent nanoprecipitates change interstitial-cluster migration from one-dimensional to more isotropic three-dimensional pathways.
The altered defect-migration pathways enhance point-defect recombination.
Enhanced point-defect recombination suppresses irradiation-induced void formation and dislocation-loop accumulation.
Coherent precipitate interfaces preserve dislocation transmission needed for plasticity.
Coherent nanoprecipitation can provide a tungsten refractory HEA with high strength and tensile ductility.
After approximately 100 dpa of simulated irradiation, the aged alloy will show more than a 50% decrease in void swelling relative to the unaged baseline.
After approximately 100 dpa of simulated irradiation, the aged alloy will show more than a 50% decrease in defect-cluster density relative to the unaged baseline.
The aged alloy will retain yield strength and ductility similar to or better than the unaged alloy after irradiation.
The nanoprecipitates will remain sufficiently stable to improve radiation tolerance at fusion-divertor operating temperatures.
Room-temperature 150 keV Ar+ irradiation is a suitable surrogate for evaluating the claimed behavior under fusion plasma-facing neutron-damage conditions.
A controlled post-sintering aging treatment preserves engineering and processing practicality.

contradictions.description: The claimed benefit is bounded to temperatures relevant to fusion-reactor/divertor operation, but the proposed decisive irradiation experiment is conducted at room temperature. A negative room-temperature result would therefore not necessarily falsify a claim explicitly conditioned on fusion-relevant operating temperatures.
